nameStory: The three-lined potato beetle gets its name from the three distinct dark stripes running down its wing covers, making it look like it's wearing a racing uniform. While it's called a "potato beetle," it's actually more commonly found munching on other plants in the nightshade family, earning its scientific name "daturaphila" from its love of jimsonweed (Datura).
description: The three-lined potato beetle is a small, oval-shaped leaf beetle about the size of a ladybug. Its most striking feature is the three bold black or dark brown stripes running lengthwise down its yellow-orange wing covers. The head and thorax are typically reddish-brown, creating a colorful contrast with the striped wing covers. These beetles are often seen crawling on leaves or flying short distances between plants.

idTips.label: Three dark stripes
idTips.description: Look for three distinct black or dark brown stripes running from head to tail along the wing covers - they're perfectly parallel and evenly spaced like lane markers on a road

idTips.label: Yellow-orange wing covers
idTips.description: The background color of the wing covers is bright yellow to orange, creating a bold contrast with the dark stripes - feels smooth and hard like plastic when gently touched

idTips.label: Reddish-brown head and thorax
idTips.description: The front section of the beetle (head and thorax) is typically reddish-brown or rust-colored, distinctly different from the striped wing covers

idTips.label: Small oval shape
idTips.description: About 6-8mm long with a classic beetle shape - dome-like and oval when viewed from above, fitting comfortably on your pinky fingernail

idTips.label: Plant association
idTips.description: Almost always found on nightshade family plants, often with small round holes chewed in the leaves nearby - look for their feeding damage as a clue

habitat: Look for three-lined potato beetles in sunny gardens, fields, and disturbed areas where nightshade family plants grow. They're particularly fond of jimsonweed, ground cherries, and sometimes potato plants, preferring areas with rich, well-drained soil. You'll often spot them along field edges, in vegetable gardens, and near farmland throughout New England's lower elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering sites in late spring and begin feeding on young nightshade plants. Look for fresh leaf damage and the first beetles becoming active on warm, sunny days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible feeding and mating on host plants. Larvae may also be present as small, dark grubs on leaf surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for winter by feeding heavily to build up fat reserves. They become less active as temperatures drop and seek sheltered overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in leaf litter, under bark, or in other protected locations. No beetle activity visible during cold months.

funFact: Despite being called a potato beetle, this species actually prefers wild nightshades over cultivated potatoes and can help gardeners by indicating the presence of potentially toxic jimsonweed - a plant so poisonous that just touching it can cause skin reactions in sensitive people!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Colorado potato beetle, but the Colorado potato beetle is much larger, has 10 black stripes instead of 3, and has a more rounded, chunky appearance. Remember: "Three lines fine, ten lines trouble" - the Colorado potato beetle is the serious agricultural pest.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this isn't the infamous potato pest that farmers worry about. That troublemaker is the Colorado potato beetle, which is much larger and more destructive. The three-lined potato beetle is relatively harmless and actually serves as a natural indicator of wild nightshade plants in your area.
compareHints: As the only Lema species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small leaf beetles like flea beetles or cucumber beetles. Unlike flea beetles which jump when disturbed, three-lined potato beetles crawl steadily and fly short distances. Unlike cucumber beetles which prefer cucumbers and squash, these stick to nightshade family plants and have much more distinct, organized striping.
